**On Walking Without Anywhere to Go**

There is a particular kind of afternoon that begins with a small act of rebellion: you put on your shoes, step outside, and set off in no direction in particular. You have no errand. You are not exercising, exactly, or if you are, that is not the point. You are not going to see anyone. You have left the house for the strange, old-fashioned purpose of leaving the house. Within a few minutes, something shifts. The shoulders drop. The breath deepens without being told to. The world, which from indoors had seemed like a task, becomes a place again.

I have come to believe that this act — walking without destination — is one of the most quietly endangered human experiences, and one of the most necessary. It is endangered because it produces nothing, because it cannot be optimized, because it fills no metric and advances no goal. It is necessary for precisely the same reasons.

Our culture has a difficult relationship with purposelessness. We speak of "wandering" the way we speak of illness, as something to be cured. A person who is "lost" is a problem to be solved. The language of modern life is saturated with destination: goals, targets, milestones, trajectories, five-year plans. Even our leisure is now described in the vocabulary of work — we "invest" in rest, we "optimize" our mornings, we take walks "for our health," which is to say, for a reason. The walk without a reason is the odd one out, the coin that will not spend. To say "I'm just walking" to a neighbor who asks where you're headed is to offer a small social provocation. Just? Just walking?

But there is a long and distinguished lineage of just walking. Aristotle and his students were called the Peripatetics, the ones who walk around, because philosophy in ancient Athens happened in motion, under the covered walkways of the Lyceum, thought unspooling at the pace of footsteps. Rousseau claimed that he could do his best thinking only on the move, and that the moment he stopped walking, the thoughts stopped too. Wordsworth, by his sister Dorothy's account, composed poetry pacing the garden path and out along the lanes, murmuring lines to himself, his body a metronome for his mind. Kierkegaard wrote that he had walked himself into his best thoughts, and that he knew of no thought so heavy that one could not walk away from it. Thoreau devoted an entire essay to the practice, "Walking," in which he confessed that he could not preserve his health and spirits unless he spent four hours a day sauntering through the woods, absolutely free from all worldly engagements. Four hours. Sauntering — a word he traced, perhaps dubiously but wonderfully, to the idle pilgrims of the Middle Ages, the saints terre, those who wandered the countryside under the pretense of going to the Holy Land, with no true destination at all.

What all of them knew, and what we keep having to rediscover, is that the mind and the feet are in conversation. There is a reason we say we need to "walk something off," or that an idea is "on its feet," or that we will "run it by" someone. Thought has a cadence. When the body moves at an easy, unforced rhythm — not the truncated shuffle of the commute, not the punishing cadence of the workout, but the loose, self-selected pace of a creature with nowhere in particular to be — the mind seems to fall into that rhythm like a child falling asleep in a car. Something loosens. Something begins to move.

Neuroscience has, in recent decades, offered a formal name for what happens next. When we are not focused on a task, the brain does not go quiet. It activates. The default mode network — a set of regions that light up precisely when we are doing nothing in particular — becomes the busiest neighborhood in the mind. This is the network of daydreams, of memories shuffled like a deck, of imagined conversations, of the self talking to itself about itself. It is where we consolidate experience, where we try on futures, where we make meaning of the thing that happened this morning or twenty years ago. It is, in a real sense, where the self is made when no one is watching. And it flourishes in the in-between times — the walk, the shower, the wait at the station — that we have recently declared open season on, filling them with podcasts and feeds and the red badges of unread messages.

I do not want to romanticize this. The wandering mind can be a difficult companion. On some walks, the default mode network serves up nothing but rehearsals of old grievances and previews of imagined disasters. The walk without destination can become a circuit of worry, the same four anxieties walked in a loop around the reservoir. Anyone who has set out to clear their head only to find the head more crowded than the kitchen they left knows this. But even this, I think, is a kind of work the mind needs to do — the churning of the unsolved, the slow digestion of experience. The walk doesn't always give us peace. Sometimes it gives us the truth that peace was never the assignment. Sometimes it just gives us room, and room is not the same as comfort.

What I love most about the aimless walk is what it does to attention. When you are going somewhere, you see the route. The mind is ahead of the body, already at the destination, and the intervening world becomes an obstacle course of turns and crossings, a thing to be gotten through. When you are going nowhere, the world is no longer in the way. It is the whole of what there is. I have walked the same streets for years, and I am still surprised by them. There is a hawthorn two blocks from my door that I did not properly see until the third year, when I happened to pass it in May, in full white bloom, looking for all the world like something from a painting I half-remembered. There is a house on the corner whose front garden is planted entirely in blue — forget-me-nots, lobelia, a painted blue door, a blue watering can — by a person I have never met and feel I know completely. There is a stretch of wall where the mortar has worn away in a pattern like a shoreline on a map of a country that does not exist. None of this is on the way to anywhere. That is why it is still visible.

The phone has changed this, as it has changed most things. I want to be fair to the phone. I carry one. I have used it to identify a bird by its song while standing in the very hedge the bird was singing from, and this seemed to me a small miracle. But the phone is a destination in the pocket. It is always somewhere else, always more interesting in principle, always offering a better world than the one at the end of the street. The aimless walk requires a certain poverty of alternatives. It requires that the here be, for a little while, the only thing on offer. Every generation before ours had this poverty forced upon them, and they filled the vacuum with looking, with thinking, with the low-grade magnificent hallucination of a mind left alone. We have abolished the vacuum. We have abolished it so thoroughly that many of us no longer remember what it felt like, and so we do not know what we have lost, the way you cannot miss a color you have never seen.

There is a deeper loss here, and it has to do with knowing places. A map knows a city as a diagram: nodes, edges, the shortest path. But a city known only by map and transit is a city known the way you might know a person only by their resume. To know a place on foot, without agenda, is to know it the way you know a friend's laugh — through accumulated, useless, concrete detail. The steepness of a particular block. The way the light comes down a certain alley at four in the afternoon in October. The shop that is always, somehow, closing. The dog that has appointed itself the supervisor of a corner. This knowledge cannot be looked up. It can only be accrued, slowly, by a body moving through a place with the leisure to be surprised by it. Every city is two cities: the one that exists for people going somewhere, and the one that exists for people going nowhere. The second city is larger. Almost no one lives there anymore.

I think often of what we do to children in this regard. A child walking with a parent who has somewhere to be is a child being trained out of the second city. "Come along." "Keep up." "Don't stop." Every step is a lesson: the world is a corridor between appointments. But watch a child who is actually allowed to wander — in a wood, on a beach, even in a cluttered backyard — and you will see attention in its natural state: total, absorbing, unproductive, delighted. The child will spend twenty minutes with a stick. The stick is not a means to anything. The stick is a universe. Somewhere in the course of being educated, useful, and on time, most of us lose the stick. The aimless walk is, among other things, an attempt to get the stick back.

I took one of these walks recently, in the hour before dusk, when the light does that thing it does in late spring — long, gold, slightly sideways, as if the sun were already tired and leaning on the horizon. I left by the back door, as I often do, into the alley. The alley is a service road for the neighborhood, a place of bins and garage doors and blackberry canes that no one planted and no one can quite bring themselves to kill. It is not scenic. That is its virtue. Because it is not scenic, no one goes there to see it, and so what you see there is what is actually there: a fox, once, sitting in the middle of the way with the composure of a landlord; a child's drawing of a sun, chalked on a garage door, half washed by rain into something that looked more like a jellyfish; the smell of cut grass coming over a fence from a garden I will never enter, carrying with it the entire concept of Sunday.

I walked without deciding, which is the whole trick. At each junction, I let the body choose, and I observed the choice with mild interest, the way you might watch a dog pick a direction on a familiar route. The body, it turns out, has opinions. It prefers the level path, the one with the tree cover, the one that loops back toward home without actually arriving there. We know our neighborhoods in our legs more than in our minds. There is a version of a map of my town that exists only in the musculature of my turns, and it is more honest than any I could draw.

Down by the old rail line, now a path, I passed a man standing perfectly still, looking up into a tree. I followed his gaze and after a long moment found the owl. We did not speak. We stood there together for perhaps four minutes, two strangers in the particular fellowship of having seen the same hidden thing, and then we walked on in opposite directions, each of us carrying the owl. This is the other gift of going nowhere: it makes you available. The scheduled self, the self with a destination, is a closed door. The unscheduled self is a door left ajar. The world comes in through the gap — the owl, the blue garden, the smell of grass, the conversation between two people on a bench that you hear only a sentence of and think about for a week.

That overheard sentence, by the way, is a literature all its own. On aimless walks I have collected more fragments of other people's lives than I know what to do with. A woman saying, "Well, that's the last time I lend her anything." A man, into a phone, with tremendous dignity, "I am doing my best, and my best is not nothing." Two teenagers, one to the other, in a tone of revolution: "What if we just didn't go?" These sentences are incomplete, which is why they lodge. The mind, given nothing to finish, finishes them. Entire novels have been written in my head on the strength of a half-heard remark and a quarter mile of empty pavement. This is the default mode network doing what it evolved to do: taking the scraps of the social world and weaving them into stories, rehearsing other lives, running the simulation of what it is to be someone else. It is how we come to have imaginations at all. It is also, I suspect, how we come to have mercy.

I do not want to overclaim. Walking will not save anyone. It will not fix what is broken in the world, and it can become its own kind of piety, its own badge, another thing to feel guilty about not doing enough of. There are people who cannot walk easily, for whom this whole meditation might read as a catalogue of inaccessible goods. The point is not the walking, exactly. The point is the mode of being the walking makes available: the unguarded attention, the willingness to be where you are, the temporary suspension of the idea that every moment must lead somewhere. You can get there other ways. Some people get there by sitting still. Some by swimming. Some by playing an instrument badly, which is a kind of wandering of the hands. Walking is simply the oldest and most democratic of these technologies, requiring no equipment beyond a door.

What I notice, when I come back from one of these walks, is a change in the texture of the hours that follow. The evening is slower. The rooms of the house seem slightly larger, as if the walk had let some air into them. Things I had been turning over — a decision, a conversation I need to have, a piece of writing that wouldn't move — have often, unaccountably, moved. Not solved. Moved. The walk does not deliver answers so much as it restores the conditions under which answers can occur: a mind that is not clenched, a self that is not performing, a small animal that has been outside and has seen the owl.

Kierkegaard said he walked himself into his best thoughts. I would put it a bit differently. I walk myself out of my worst ones — out of the tight ones, the first-person ones, the ones that circle the drain of me. Out there, in the gold light, with no destination and therefore no narrative to defend, I become briefly a thing among things: a body, a shadow, a passerby, a witness of an owl and a chalk jellyfish and a stranger doing his best. The world does not need this of me. That is the point. Almost nothing out there needs anything of me, and so, for an hour, I am free.

Then I come home, and the kettle goes on, and the world's claims resume. But some residue of the unscheduled hour clings, the way the smell of cut grass clings to a sleeve. And I find that I am, for a while, a slightly better inhabitant of my own life — more the child with the stick, less the commuter on the corridor. Which is, I think, as good a use of an afternoon as any, and better than most.
